answer: A CDN sits transparently between the user and the origin. The origin is a generic term for wherever the content lives: an S3 bucket, a backend server, literally anything you want served through the CDN. The CDN serves cached bytes if it has them; on a miss it fetches the same path from the origin. In the simplest setup the origin must be publicly accessible (with security policies, depending on the CDN).
evidence: Ch2 §2.1: 'A CDN transparently sits between your user and your origin.' 'Origin is a generic term for wherever the content lives: an S3 bucket, a backend server, literally anything you want served through your CDN.'

answer: A CDN is not something you push things to. Most CDNs offer APIs nowadays, but that is not their main job; their job is to sit transparently between the user and the origin. It pulls: on a miss it fetches from the origin itself.
evidence: Ch2 §2.1: 'A CDN is not something you push things to. Most CDNs offer APIs nowadays, but that is not their main job. Their job is to sit transparently between the user and the origin.' 'Nothing is pushed to it: it pulls.'

answer: The backend's bandwidth is spent on something almost static (an image hardly ever changes), and images are huge (1, 2, 3, 5, 10 MB) - spending 10 MB of an API server's bandwidth to serve one is 'a crime'. The bytes leave through the same network card every API call needs; you want API servers lean and fast. Distance makes it worse: a server in Singapore sending 10 MB to a user in the US slows everything down.
evidence: Ch2 §2.1 + Fig 2·a: 'images are huge: 1, 2, 3, 5, 10 MB. Spending 10 MB of an API server's bandwidth to serve one of them is "a crime". You want your API servers lean and fast.'

answer: A CDN property: a single mapping of your subdomain on the provider (e.g. a.mycdn.net) to an origin (e.g. arpitbhayani.me); all it asks for is one origin URL. Any request to a.mycdn.net is forwarded to the origin. Akamai calls it a property, CloudFront a distribution. To use your own hostname you add a DNS CNAME pointing to the CDN's edge hostname.
evidence: Ch2 §2.2: 'All it asks for is one origin URL... That configuration is a mapping, called a CDN property: your subdomain on the provider, say a.mycdn.net, mapped to an origin, arpitbhayani.me.'

answer: Through ordinary DNS: the browser resolves whatever hostname is in the URL; a.mycdn.net resolves to the CDN provider's IP address (classic DNS configuration on Route 53 or your domain provider such as GoDaddy/Namecheap; a CNAME to the CDN's edge hostname), and the browser sends the request to that IP. It neither knows nor needs to know it is a CDN.
evidence: Ch2 §2.2: 'The browser doesn't know whether a host is a CDN... it does a DNS resolution of whatever hostname is in the URL and sends the request to that IP address. Resolving a.mycdn.net returns the CDN provider's IP address.'

answer: 1) The browser asks DNS for a.mycdn.net and gets the CDN's IP. 2) It sends GET /system-design/logo.png to the CDN. 3) The CDN checks whether it has anything cached for this path - no, first request (miss). 4) It looks up the origin configured for the property (a.mycdn.net -> arpitbhayani.me), discards its own host, keeps the path. 5) The CDN itself requests arpitbhayani.me/system-design/logo.png; the origin generates the response as it always does. 6) The CDN caches the bytes and returns them to the user.
evidence: Ch2 §2.2 Fig 2·c steps; §2.3: 'do I have anything cached for this path? No, it is the first request. So the CDN itself makes the request to arpitbhayani.me/system-design/logo.png... which caches it and sends it to the user.'

answer: The host changes: the CDN discards its own hostname (a.mycdn.net) and puts the configured origin (arpitbhayani.me) in its place. The path stays exactly the same. That is why any path under the property works without configuring individual URLs.
evidence: Ch2 §2.2: 'It swaps the host and keeps the path: a.mycdn.net/system-design/logo.png becomes arpitbhayani.me/system-design/logo.png.'

answer: It is a cache hit: the CDN already has the image cached and serves it directly; the request never enters the backend. The origin hears from the CDN again only when the cached copy expires (or is invalidated).
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'This time the CDN already has the image cached and serves it directly.' Clip 2·1: 'Every later request is a hit. The origin never hears about it. When the copy expires, one request refills it.'

answer: No. The CDN caches whatever it gets back as a set of bytes: API responses, JSON, text files, images, videos, fragments. Caveat: it won't cache everything automatically - the response must be cacheable per the origin's headers (Cache-Control max-age/s-maxage; not no-store/private) and the CDN's policy; e.g. Cloudflare doesn't cache HTML or JSON by default and skips private/no-store/no-cache/max-age=0/Set-Cookie responses unless cache rules make them eligible.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'API responses, JSON responses, text files, images, videos, fragments: all of them can be cached on a CDN. What a CDN won't do is cache everything automatically.'

answer: On a hit the request doesn't even enter your backend, saving the backend servers' bandwidth and cutting infrastructure cost: you need a couple of servers instead of hundreds, since only a few requests reach the backend (each time the cache invalidates). It gives efficiency and takes load off the backend. Rule of thumb: you keep infra cost down while paying almost the same to the CDN, and get extra performance on top; actual savings depend on traffic and hit ratio.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'You need a couple of servers instead of hundreds... you keep your infrastructure cost down while paying almost the same amount to the CDN, and get extra performance on top; the actual savings depend on your traffic and your hit ratio.'
